name: memory-sustained-heap-growth
capturedFrom:
probe/bloc_probe with `--dart-define=scenario=memory`, device A015 (Android 16, Flutter 3.44.1) over adb TCP, 2026-08-28. ~33-second window: idle, then 300 steps appending ~4,000 strings each to a list held for the app's lifetime, then idle while still holding all of it. Recorded with `capture-mem.mjs`, which calls `get_memory` twelve times at 2.5s intervals — memory samples only enter the store when something asks for one, so a plain connect-and-wait capture records none and this hypothesis can never fire.

`session.clockOffsetMs` is -839ms: the phone's clock runs behind the recorder's by most of a second. Nothing here depends on cross-clock ordering — the argument is a monotone series compared against itself — but it is worth seeing in a fixture, because it is nearly a third of the engine's 3s correlation window.
why:
The right answer is `memory`, and the point of recording it is the shape of the series rather than its size.

Twelve samples, strictly monotonic, no drop anywhere: 88.99MB rising to 216.72MB (144%) over roughly thirty seconds. That monotonicity is the whole argument. Dart's heap grows between collections, so a growing heap on its own means nothing — a healthy app under load produces a sawtooth, climbing and then falling back as the collector runs. Twelve consecutive rises with not one fall is not a sawtooth. Something is holding references, and here that is literally true: the probe appends to a list it never releases.

Two further fields in the same samples rule out the obvious misreadings. `externalUsageMB` is 0 in every one of the twelve, so the growth is Dart heap and not external allocation accounted elsewhere — which is why the probe retains strings rather than a `Uint8List`, whose bytes can land in the external counter and prove nothing about the heap. And `heapCapacityMB` climbs with usage, 92.36MB to 216.36MB: the VM kept expanding the heap to accommodate live data rather than reclaiming it. A heap that was merely un-collected would sit inside a capacity that stayed put.

Nothing competes. 5 of 432 frames missed budget (1.2%), far under the 20% the jank hypothesis requires — worth stating because allocation pressure could easily have produced collection pauses and made this a jank session instead, and the workload is deliberately paced in small steps so it does not. Zero exceptions, zero network events, and the diagnosis reports no alternative causes at all. `diagnose_performance` separately calls the session healthy at 0.8, which is correct: frames were fine throughout.

Confidence 0.75 is the higher of the two values this hypothesis can produce, awarded for growth at or above 100%. It is still the lowest-priority hypothesis in the engine and it should stay there. What is being pinned is deliberately modest: the summary says `Dart heap grew`, the root cause says `Sustained heap growth`, and the first recommended fix opens `Growth is not proof of a leak`. This incident must not be read as evidence that the tool detects leaks. It detects a monotone series and declines to call it more than that, and that restraint is as much a part of the expected answer as the label is.

The anchor is the newest sample, and it must be cited: a growth claim whose evidence does not include the reading it ends at cannot be checked.

collectors.name: state
collectors.detail: No state-management activity observed yet. Riverpod posts riverpod:new_event and provider posts provider:provider_changed when dependents are notified (which is the only way a flutter_bloc app shows up, since bloc itself posts nothing). An app using none of them, and one that simply has not changed state yet, look the same from here, so an empty result never proves an app has no blocs.

runtime.summary: Dart heap grew from 88.99MB to 216.72MB (144%) across 12 samples.
runtime.rootCause: Sustained heap growth: 88.99MB → 216.72MB over the session.
limitations: No network evidence in this session. HTTP capture is pull-on-demand and Dart-side only — platform-code and WebView traffic is never visible.
VM timeline events are fetched on demand and not stored, so they take no part in correlation.
Only Dart-side runtime state is observed. A cause in platform (Kotlin/Swift) code or in a WebView cannot appear here.

confidenceBreakdown.basis: Conservative heuristic scored from corroborating evidence, not a calibrated probability. Below 0.7 the status is "unknown" rather than a guess.

recommendedFixes: Growth is not proof of a leak — Dart's heap grows between collections. Compare against heap capacity and re-sample after activity settles.
If growth does not plateau, look for retained listeners, controllers, or images that are never disposed.

performance.summary: 5/432 frames (1%) exceeded the 16.67ms budget — within normal range.
limitations: No CPU sampling. A slow build can be attributed to a widget, but not to a specific function — use the DevTools CPU profiler for that.
GC events are not observable: the VM timeline is fetched on demand and not stored, so garbage-collection pauses cannot be ruled in or out.
Frames are only captured while connected, and older ones roll out of the retention window.

No state-management activity observed. Riverpod and provider announce on the Extension stream (a flutter_bloc app surfaces through provider, since its notifications go through it); stock bloc announces nothing of its own. An app using none of them looks identical to one that simply has not changed state.
Rebuild totals cover the busiest locations in each frame, not every rebuild — the long tail is counted but not itemised.
App-versus-package attribution is a path heuristic: getPubRootDirectories is empty until a DevTools client sets it, so there is no authoritative project root.

notes: No route changes captured. Navigator posts Flutter.Navigation on push/pop, so either nothing has navigated since connecting, or the app is a release build.
